## Background {#sec-setup}
There are plenty of ways to define the Fourier Transform, but here we'll define the 
Fourier Transform of a function $u\in L^2[0,2\pi]$ as
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{F}[u](x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\hat{u} e^{inx}\quad(\star)\\
\text{where}\ \hat{u}_n=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(x)e^{-inx}dx.
\end{align*}
$\mathcal{F}[u](x)$ is the Fourier Representation of $u$, and $\hat{u}_n$ are the Fourier coefficients.
Our truncated Fourier Representation $\mathcal{F}_N$ is defined as 
$$
\mathcal{F}_N[u](x)=\sum_{|n|\le N}\hat{u}_n e^{inx}.
$$

### Quick Remarks:
If we define an inner product $\inner{f}{g}:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f\bar{g}dx$, 
the set $\{e^{inx}: n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is orthanormal with respect to the above inner product 
\begin{align*}
\inner{e^{imx}}{e^{inx}} &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(m-n)x}\,dx
  = \frac{1}{2\pi i(m-n)} e^{i(m-n)x}\bigg|_0^{2\pi} = 0, \quad m\neq n, \\
\inner{e^{inx}}{e^{inx}} &= 1.
\end{align*}
Notice $\hat{u}_n = \inner{u}{e^{inx}}$, so each of our Fourier terms is a projection of $u$ 
onto one of our basis funcitons, i.e. the Fourier basis.

By the completeness of $L_2$ and the Fourier basis, we get the equality of $(\star)$. 

*We will show this some other time*

## Discritizaiton {#sec-discritizaiton}

Suppose we have a function $f$ on the real interval $[0,2\pi]$, then we can discritize the
interval with $2N + 1$ points where $x_j = j(\frac{2\pi}{2N+1})$ and $j\in[2N]$. Additionally, 
we would like to interpolate the funciton values at each $x_j$, i.e.
$$
f(x_j)=\sum_{|k|\le N} \hat{f}_k e^{ikx_j}.
$$
Let $\mathbf E$ be a $(2N+1)\times (2N+1)$ matrix such that $(E)_{j m} = e^{ik x_j}$ where $j\in[2N]$ corresponds 
to the row indices and $m\in[2N]$ corresponds to column indices such that $m=1\mapsto k= -N,\ \dots,\ m= 2N+1 \mapsto k=N$.
Then let $\mathbf{\hat{f}}=(\hat{f}_{-N},\dots, \hat{f}_N)^T$ and we can represent our interpolation scheme as
$$
\mathbf E\mathbf{\hat{f}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})
$$
where $\mathbf E$ is called the Fourier Matrix. 

::: {#thm-fourier_matrix_orth}
.  $\mathbf E$ is orthoganal.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let our discritizaiton scheme from above hold. We will show $\mathbf E^* \mathbf E$ is a diagonal matrix. Let $(\mathbf E^*)_{\ell_1,:}$ 
denote a row of $\mathbf E^*$ and $(\mathbf E)_{:, \ell_2}$ denote a column of $\mathbf E$. Then,
we have two cases.

$Case \ 1:\ (\ell_1=\ell_2)$. 
\begin{align*}
(\mathbf E^* \mathbf E)_{\ell_1, \ell_1} 
&= \sum_{j=0}^{2N}e^{-i\ell_1 x_j}e^{i\ell_2 x_j}\\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{2N}e^{i(-\ell_1+\ell_2)x_j} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{2N} 1 = 2N+1
\end{align*}

$Case \ 2:\ (\ell_1\ne \ell_2)$
\begin{align*}
(\mathbf E^* \mathbf E)_{\ell_1, \ell_1} 
&= \sum_{j=0}^{2N}e^{-i\ell_1 x_j}e^{i\ell_2 x_j}\\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{2N}e^{i(-\ell_1+\ell_2)x_j} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{2N}e^{i(-\ell_1+\ell_2)(\frac{2\pi}{2N+1})j}\\
&= \bigg(\frac{1-e^{i(\ell_2-\ell_1)2\pi}}{1-e^{i(-\ell_1+\ell_2)(\frac{2\pi}{2N+1})}}   \bigg)=0
\end{align*}
since
$$
|e^{i(-\ell_1+\ell_2)(\frac{2\pi}{2N+1})}|< 1\quad\text{and}\quad e^{i(\ell_2-\ell_1)2\pi}=1.
$$
Hence $\mathbf E^* \mathbf E=\frac{1}{2N+1}\mathbf I$.
:::

::: {#cor-dft}
## Discrete Fourier Transform

The Discrete Fourier Transform is given by 
$$
\hat f_k = \frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{j=0}^{2N} f(x_j)e^{-ikx_j}
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\mathbf E \mathbf{\hat f} = \mathbf f$. Multiplying by $\mathbf E^*$ on the left yeilds, 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf E^* \mathbf E \mathbf{\hat f}&=\mathbf E^* \mathbf f\\
\mathbf{\hat f}&=\frac{1}{2N+1}\mathbf E^* \mathbf f
\end{align*}
which implies the corollary above.
:::

## Differentiation {#sec-differentiation}

In the computational setting differential operators get discritized, i.e. they become matrices.
Lets consider a discritizaiton with $N$ points and $f$ as above
\begin{align*}
f(x)&\approx \sum_{n\in S_n}\hat{f}_n e^{inx}& S_n=\begin{cases}-\frac{N}{2},\dots,\frac{N}{2}-1&if\ N\ even\\ -\frac{N-1}{2},\dots,\frac{N-1}{2}&if \ N\ odd\end{cases}\\
\hat{f}_n&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} f(x_j)e^{-inx_j}&x_j = j\frac{2\pi}{N}.
\end{align*}
Then
$$
\mathbf D_N^{m}f(x_j)\approx \sum_{n\in S_n}\hat{f}_n (in)^m e^{inx},
$$
which can be represented as matrix vector multiplicaiton
\begin{align*}
\mathbf D_N^{m}\mathbf f
&\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\mathbf E\mathrm{diag}((in)^m, \dots, (in)^m)\mathbf{\hat f}\\
&=\frac{1}{N}\mathbf E\ \mathbf{\mathrm{diag}}((in)^m, \dots, (in)^m)\ \mathbf E^*\mathbf f
\end{align*}
by @cor-dft. Then we get $\mathbf D_N^{m}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbf E\ \mathbf{\mathrm{diag}}((in)^m, \dots, (in)^m)\ \mathbf E^*$,
which is the eigen-decomposition of $\mathbf D_N^{m}$ in the Fourier basis. 

Notice the eigenvalue of $\mathbf D_N^{m}$ are real and negative when $m$ is even and strictly imaginary when $m$ is odd.

## PDEs {#sec-PDEs}
Consider the 1-D transport equation $u_t=u_{x}$, then by discritizing the PDE we get 
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\overrightarrow{u}(t)=\mathbf D_N\overrightarrow{u}(t).
$$
Indeed $\mathbf D_N$ has complex eigenvalues in the Fourier basis. Further, 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf D_N \mathbf D_N^*
&=\frac{1}{N^2}\mathbf E\ \mathbf{\mathrm{diag}}((in)^m, \dots, (in)^m)\ \mathbf E^*(\mathbf E\ \mathbf{\mathrm{diag}}((in)^m, \dots, (in)^m)\ \mathbf E^*)^*\\
&=\mathbf I
\end{align*}
so let $\mathbf x, \mathbf y\in\mathbb{R}^N$, then $\|\mathbf D_N \mathbf x -\mathbf D_N \mathbf y\|=\|\mathbf D_N(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)\|=\|\mathbf x-\mathbf y\|$. 
Hence, as an operator $\mathbf D_N$ preserves rigid motions in euclidian space, as expected by the transport equation.


Now consider the 1-D diffusion equation $u_t=u_{xx}$, then by discritizing the PDE we get
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\overrightarrow{u}(t)=\mathbf D^2_N\overrightarrow{u}(t).
$$
Since $\mathbf D^2_N$ has real negative eigenvalues, from the ODE perspective we can think of the PDE as decaying to 
a fixed point in the Fourier basis, i.e. the $k=0$ wavenumber.
